☆ Topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition
Luca Rizzi, Giuditta Rovelli
We study the topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition on length-minimizing curves in the metric tangent space. We prove that sufficiently small spheres are Lipschitz hypersurfaces homeomorphic to Euclidean spheres, while closed balls are homeomorphic to Euclidean closed balls, and open balls are diffeomorphic to Euclidean open balls. These results improve the known ones and extend them beyond two-step distributions. The proof relies on uniform Lipschitz estimates for the distance, of independent interest.
☆ Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks
Yuanxiang Yang, Yu Liu, Fabricio Oliveira, Yu Han, Claudio Roncoli
Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a Bézier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
☆ Variable Metric Three Operator Splitting
Hansol Suh, Tobin Isaac
To minimize the sum $f + g + h$ of three convex functions when $f$ is differentiable with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient, we present a proximal algorithm, variable-metric three operator splitting (VMTOS), a generalization of the three operator splitting (TOS) scheme of Davis and Yin. We establish convergence guarantees by controlling changes in the metric. The smallest saddle-point residual among the first $k$ primal-dual iterates is $\tilde{O}(k^{-1/2})$. When $f$ and the convex conjugate $h^*$ are strongly convex and the accepted metrics and their inverses are uniformly bounded, the rate improves to $\tilde{O}(β^k)$ for some $β\in (0,1)$. We develop a practical Barzilai--Borwein update for diagonal metrics that satisfies our bound on metric changes. Under the same strong convexity assumptions, this update guarantees the required uniform metric bounds, yielding R-linear convergence. Numerical experiments on benchmark optimization problems show that VMTOS is competitive with other proximal algorithms.
☆ Controllability of Nonlocal Partial Differential Equations
D. Cardona, S. E. Chorfi, F. Et-tahri, L. Maniar
This chapter provides a short survey of recent developments in the controllability of nonlocal partial differential equations. We first review controllability results for evolution equations involving nonlocal spatial operators. Particular attention is devoted to unique continuation properties, observability inequalities, and Carleman estimates in establishing controllability properties. We then discuss controllability issues for partial differential equations with memory terms, highlighting how memory effects influence reachable states, null controllability, and exact controllability. We review and compare various analytical techniques developed to overcome the difficulties arising from the nonlocal structure. We also provide a critical assessment of some of these methods. Throughout the chapter, we emphasize the interplay between controllability and observability, the adaptation of classical control methods to nonlocal settings, and the distinctive phenomena that arise in comparison with local equations. We then discuss geometric inequalities and their role in the controllability of diffusion models. The chapter concludes with a discussion of current challenges and several open problems, aiming to provide directions for future research.
☆ Continuous Envy-Free Allocation via Reciprocal Preference Matrices: An Alternative to Sperner-Based Discretization
Luis Ángel Calvo Pascual, Susana Merchán Rubira, Diego de Pereda Sebastián, Javier Rodrigo Hitos
Fair allocation problems on a continuous simplex are often approached through Sperner-type discretizations: agents label mesh vertices according to their preferences and a fully labelled elementary triangle gives a discrete localization of a fair outcome. We develop a continuous alternative for three agents and three alternatives by representing preferences with multiplicatively consistent reciprocal pairwise-comparison matrices. Two independent ratios per agent induce exact linear indifference boundaries and turn envy-free allocation into a finite-dimensional feasibility problem. For the six possible assignments, we introduce an assignment score $Φ$ built from the agents' consistent priority vectors and prove that an incentive solution component is nonempty if and only if its assignment is the unique minimizer of $Φ$, whereas a disincentive solution component is nonempty if and only if its assignment is the unique maximizer. Consequently, the strict solution region is either empty or a unique convex preference region whose closure lies in the interior of the simplex. The weak solution set is never empty and degenerates exactly when $Φ$ has ties. We also compare the exact continuous formulation with Sperner-based discretization, including the boundary convention required in the disincentive model. Under exact consistency, the model uses six independent pairwise thresholds, whereas a regular triangular mesh with resolution $m$ contains $(m+1)(m+2)/2$ vertices. The method therefore exchanges a stronger parametric preference assumption for an exact continuous solution set and a resolution-independent elicitation stage.
☆ A Retrospective-Approximation Interior-Point Method
Frank E. Curtis, Zahra Khatti, Daniel P. Robinson
An algorithm is proposed, analyzed, and tested for solving nonlinearly constrained continuous optimization problem instances wherein the objective function is defined by an expectation over a random variable argument and the constraints include inequalities (and perhaps equalities) involving functions that may be nonconvex. The algorithm combines a retrospective-approximation strategy for handling the objective and an interior-point approach for handling the constraints. In each iteration of an outer loop, the objective is approximated by an empirical average over a set of realizations of the random variable argument and the resulting sampled problem is solved with an interior-point method that allows inexact search-direction computations for computational flexibility. Termination conditions for the interior-point method are tailored for those needed for convergence guarantees by the outer loop. Over the outer loop, the sample set is updated adaptively in such a manner that convergence guarantees for solving the original optimization problem can be assured. The results of numerical experiments are presented, which show that the proposed algorithm can outperform competing methods that have comparable theoretical guarantees.
☆ A Feasible-Direction-Type Method for Nonconvex Optimization with Infeasible Starts
Danlin Li, Johannes Milz
We develop an infeasible-start extension of the Topkis--Veinott feasible-direction method for nonconvex composite optimization. At each main iteration, a strongly convex local model is used to obtain objective descent while limiting increases in constraint violation. A separate feasibility-reduction step is invoked when feasibility improvement is needed. Under a feasibility-reduction condition, we establish the standard first-order rate for reducing the Fritz John residual and constraint violation. We then verify that both proximal-gradient and regularized Gauss--Newton methods applied to minimizing the squared constraint-violation function satisfy the required feasibility-reduction property under a Polyak--Łojasiewicz condition. Numerical experiments compare the reduction methods, including an experimental prox-linear variant, and compare the scalar-regularized and curvature-enhanced subproblem formulations.

☆ Safeguarded Neurally-Accelerated Preconditioning (SNAP) framework for Nonlinear Optimization
Youngkyu Lee, George Em Karniadakis, Alena Kopaničáková
We introduce the Safeguarded Neurally-Accelerated Preconditioning (SNAP) framework for hybridizing nonlinear optimization methods with pre-trained neural operators (NOs). SNAP targets parametric optimization problems arising from variational formulations of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), where many parameter instances require repeated solves. Inspired by multilevel line-search methods, SNAP operates in cycles, combining classical optimization steps with a search direction generated by a pre-trained NO. Since NO-generated search directions carry no a priori descent guarantee, SNAP employs an a posteriori safeguard by accepting only corrections that satisfy prescribed descent and acceptance conditions. We prove global convergence of the SNAP algorithm and show that it preserves the convergence rate of the underlying optimization method independently of the employed NO architecture. Moreover, we also show that when the NO corrections are sufficiently accurate, SNAP converges faster, with the improvement directly related to the NO training error. To demonstrate SNAP's efficiency in practice, we run numerical experiments on a diverse set of nonlinear parametric optimization problems, including parametric minimal surface, Allen--Cahn, and nonlinear Helmholtz problems. The efficiency of SNAP is demonstrated by comparing two NO architectures, Fourier neural operator (FNO) and Transolver, and by using SNAP as a standalone solver and as a nonlinear preconditioner. Our numerical results show a substantial reduction in the number of required iterations, while demonstrating robustness and generalization across a wide range of problem parameters and mesh resolutions.

☆ Rennala NSGD: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Beyond Euclidean Geometry NeurIPS 2026
Igor Sokolov, Alexander Tyurin, Peter Richtárik
The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $κ$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $κ$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($κ=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.

☆ cuPDQPx: A GPU-Accelerated Restarted Halpern PDHG for Large-Scale Convex Quadratic Programming
Haihao Lu, Zedong Peng, Jinwen Yang
We present cuPDQPx, a GPU-accelerated, factorization-free first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming (QP). Building on the restarted reflected Halpern primal-dual framework of cuPDLPx, we introduce an auxiliary-variable splitting that yields explicit updates without linearizing the quadratic objective or solving inner quadratic subproblems. A preconditioned proximal point interpretation yields both sublinear and linear fixed-point residual convergence guarantees. For practical efficiency, cuPDQPx integrates diagonal preconditioning, step-size selection, adaptive restart, and adaptive primal and quadratic weight updates. cuPDQPx is implemented in C and CUDA with optimized sparse matrix-vector products, kernel fusion, and CUDA Graphs. Numerical experiments on the Maros-Mészáros collection, a convex subset of QPLIB, and synthetic large-scale QPs demonstrate that cuPDQPx has strong numerical performance at both $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-8}$ tolerances.
☆ Optimality Conditions and Solution Set Characterisations of Convex Minimal Time Optimisation Problems
Doan Huu Hieu, Nguyen Duy Cuong
The paper studies convex minimisation problems involving a composition of a coordinatewise nondecreasing convex function with a finite family of nonnegative, locally Lipschitz continuous and convex functions. We establish complete dual optimality conditions and characterise the entire solution set using multipliers and subgradients associated with a given solution. The results are applied to norm optimisation problems involving minimal time functions with different convex dynamics sets and convex target sets. The sum, maximum and p-norms yield minimal time versions of the Fermat--Torricelli, Chebyshev centre and p-Fermat--Torricelli problems, respectively. Examples in finite and infinite dimensional spaces are provided to illustrate the solution set characterisations.

☆ The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Segmentation Layer
Galia Akl, Laurent Najman, Hugues Talbot
Can a Watershed transform, the classical tool of morphological segmentation, be placed at the end of a deep network and trained through? The Power Watershed (PW) is the limit of the seeded Random Walker (RW) as p grows to infinity with edge weights raised to the power p. At every finite p the RW solves a sparse positive-definite linear system and is exactly differentiable with respect to the edge weights and the unaries through one adjoint solve; its multi-label form costs one right-hand side per label, and its limit is the PW. We study this family as the last layer of a segmentation network, the watershed layer (WS layer). A conditioning study measures how the solve, the gradient and the distance to the limit evolve with p, and the implicit gradient is checked against unrolling. On synthetic data with correct edge costs the WS layer transforms a soft prediction into an exact boundary. On nuclei segmentation (PanNuke), a binary WS layer is level with a thresholded U-Net. With the instances as labels, the WS layer turns the U-Net into an instance segmenter whose number of labels is set per image by the markers rather than by the output layout, and the network is trained through that partition: instance F1 score rises from 0.656 to 0.795 over a U-Net with connected components, level with the same network followed by a tuned marker watershed. At the training temperature the partition is a watershed of the learned costs, and the finite temperature lets the solve hedge, discounting weak markers and sharing contested pixels. The hedging puts the WS layer 0.015--0.020 F1 ahead of the baseline when trained on a tenth of the data, at the price of having to deploy the finite-p solve rather than its exact limit at inference. Code and the full experimental record are released.

Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.

Nicola Cavallucci, Enrico Le Donne, Sebastiano Nicolussi Golo
We construct an explicit length-minimizing curve in a polynomial rank-two sub-Riemannian structure on $\R^4$. The example admits a minimizing lift to a rank-two Carnot group of step five. Generalizations are announced.

☆ Stable Dynamical Mass Transportation via port-Hamiltonian Structure
Dongjun Wu, Yankai Lin, Gang Feng
Dynamical optimal mass transportation over nonlinear systems is often hindered by the curse of dimensionality and open-loop implementation. We propose an alternative framework that sacrifices exact optimality in favor of stability, robustness, and scalability. We use a stochastic port-Hamiltonian system as a reference model. Under suitable structural assumptions, we show that its density converges asymptotically to a prescribed steady-state distribution. We then shape a deterministic nonlinear system into a compatible port-Hamiltonian form and add a local density-feedback term so that its closed-loop continuity equation matches the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equation of the reference model. The resulting feedback drives a broad class of initial distributions to the target distribution. Because the density term is local at the particle level, the controller admits decentralized implementation and avoids solving a global finite-horizon transport problem online. Nonlinear examples and simulations illustrate the method. For linear systems with Gaussian targets, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for stabilizing density feedback and give explicit controller constructions.
☆ Using delays for prescribed-time static output feedback stabilization of LTI controllable and observable systems
Kang-Kang Zhang, Emilia Fridman
This paper addresses a stabilization problem: can every controllable and observable LTI system be stabilized by static output feedback? To the best of our knowledge, we provide, for the first time, a solution to this problem. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves prescribed-time convergence to the origin, with the convergence time arbitrarily assigned a priori and independently of the initial condition. Two static output-feedback methods are developed. The first employs multiple artificial output delays with smooth time-varying gains and provides an explicit gain construction for every controllable and observable LTI system, based on a generalized controllability--observability Gramian introduced in this paper. The second combines constant-gain feedback of the current output with time-varying-gain feedback of a single artificially delayed output and also applies to every controllable and observable LTI system. Its simpler structure requires auxiliary parameters whose existence is guaranteed but whose explicit construction is not provided for general MIMO systems; for SISO systems, the constant current-output gain can be readily selected. The multiple-delay design is further extended to known bounded and fast-varying (without any constraints on the delay derivative) measurement delays, yielding fixed-time stabilization under a corresponding rank condition, with an assignable settling-time bound greater than three times the delay bound. For unknown constant measurement delays, fixed-time stabilization is established for systems with nilpotent state matrices. A numerical implementation is also presented. Numerical examples involving nonminimum-phase, flexible-structure, and cart--pole systems illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

☆ Controllability-Based Input Allocation in Quantum System
Riku Yaegashi, Kazuhiro Sato, Kentaro Ohki
Understanding how local perturbations influence global quantum dynamics is important for analyzing and designing large-scale quantum systems. Existing quantum centrality measures often rely on static correlations or entanglement and do not directly capture perturbation propagation under unitary evolution. We formulate controllability allocation scoring for quantum input-output dynamics governed by the Schrodinger equation. Using the multiobservable quantum-control Gramian, we introduce virtual local Hamiltonian perturbations along a nominal trajectory and decompose the terminal-output response into channel-wise Gramian contributions. A simplex-constrained log-determinant optimization combines these contributions to define a volumetric controllability allocation score (V-CAS), specifying an optimal allocation of virtual input intensities among local Hamiltonian perturbation directions. The score measures their cooperative dynamical influence and depends on the output and trajectory. We characterize the output Gramian's range and minimum-energy properties and derive a drift-independent sufficient condition ensuring score uniqueness for almost every terminal time at which the problem is feasible. For quantum many-body systems, we develop a matrix-product-state and time-evolving-block-decimation implementation that avoids explicitly constructing exponentially large state-transition matrices. We also derive an error bound propagating Trotter and MPS-truncation errors to the discrete output Gramian. Numerical experiments show that the score captures finite-time influence patterns distinct from those identified by static correlation- and entanglement-based measures and can inform target-independent control-channel preselection.

Kirill Novoselov, Yuriy Dorn, Darina Dvinskikh, Alexander Gasnikov
We study the minimax complexity of smooth convex stochastic optimization with intermittent communication: $m$ workers run for $N$ rounds, and between consecutive communication rounds each worker makes $K$ sequential stochastic gradient queries. We focus on the interpolation regime, in which all sample losses share a common minimizer, so that the gradient noise vanishes at the solution. Let $L$ be the smoothness of the objective, $H_s\ge L$ the smoothness of the sample losses, and $R$ the distance from the initial point to a minimizer. We consider three oracle models that provide increasing information: an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle $g(x,ξ)$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}_ξ\|g(x,ξ)\|^2 \leq 2H_s\bigl(F(x)-F(x^*)\bigr)$, gradients of the sample losses at fresh samples, and repeated gradient queries to stored samples. Up to logarithmic factors, all our results are described by two rates: \[ R^2\min\left\{L,\;\frac{H_s}{KN},\; \frac{L}{N^2}+\frac{H_s}{mKN}\right\} \qquad\text{and}\qquad R^2\min\left\{L,\; \frac{\min\{L,H_s/K\}}{N^2}+\frac{H_s}{mKN}\right\}, \] Under the weak growth condition, the first rate is the minimax rate, attained by the best of three simple baselines, as in the classical bounded-variance setting. With repeated access to samples, the second rate becomes the minimax rate for general convex objectives. For general convex objectives with fresh sample gradients, the minimax rate lies between the two rates. Our lower bounds apply to arbitrary randomized intermittent-communication algorithms.
☆ Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
Matthew Zurek, Yudong Chen, Josiah P. Hanna
Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $γ=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

Proximal-gradient methods are widely used for composite optimization, but inexact proximal updates introduce a residual in the proximal optimality condition, complicating the analysis of how stationarity changes across a step. We study this question for composite objectives consisting of a smooth convex term and a possibly nonsmooth weakly convex term, focusing on the relationship between the directional-stationarity measures at the input and output points of an inexact proximal-gradient step. We first establish separate input and output bounds, but their combination can yield a conservative estimate because their worst-case residual directions may differ. By exploiting the magnitude and orientation of this shared residual, we establish tight joint bounds and derive an exact one-step stationarity-transfer factor that strictly improves the estimate from separate bounds in the short-step regime. We also identify the precise residual-tolerance threshold for finite uniform stationarity transfer. A further distinction emerges over multiple steps: endpoint worst cases can repeat over arbitrarily many iterations, whereas interior worst cases cannot persist across two consecutive steps, yielding strict two-step submultiplicativity. These results also provide principled tolerance-selection rules, descent estimates, and stationarity-complexity guarantees for inexact proximal-gradient methods.

☆ Damped stochastic mirror descent for non-smooth ill-posed problems in Banach space
Harshit Bajpai, Gaurav Mittal, Ankik Kumar Giri
We introduce a damped variant of the stochastic mirror descent method for systems of non-smooth nonlinear ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces. At each iteration, the method samples a random subset of the equations, performs a mirror-descent step in the dual space with an adaptive step size derived from the discrepancy principle, and applies a damping term that prevents the iterates from drifting away from the initial guess. The scheme accommodates non-smooth forward operators through a family of bounded linear surrogates, admits general $p$-convex penalty functionals which also includes trained convex penalty, allows the noise level to differ from equation to equation, and dispenses with two classical requirements, namely reflexivity of the image space and Gâteaux differentiability of the forward operator. We study its regularization properties under an \textit{a posteriori} stopping rule by proving first that the iteration terminates after finitely many steps almost surely, and then that the mean-square error of the iterates tends to zero as the noise level vanishes. Numerical experiments on a system of non-smooth semilinear inverse source problems and the identification of a diffusion coefficient confirm the theoretical analysis and shows improved convergence results.

Fast inference and strict constraint satisfaction are essential for learning-based decision-making. Existing methods often rely on constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations, while iterative repair can be costly. We introduce Convex-SKM-Net, a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles without constraint-specific inequality projectors. It applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent (dual PGD) to minimum-displacement block problems using GPU-friendly matrix operations. We jointly learn the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality. We prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. All our test outputs on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a $10^{-3}$ feasibility tolerance. Comparisons with the latest constraint-satisfaction methods show inference speedups of up to $144.3\times$ on SOC-MPC and $7.7\times$ on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark with joint training. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is $0.012\%$, with full test feasibility at $10^{-4}$. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by $22.4\%$ and improves gaps in matched power-system comparisons.

Sikai Cheng, Tinghan Ye, Arnaud Deza, Xiaonan Qi, Miao Li, Litong Liu, Changkun Guan
Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

We continue the study of minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds--Shepp pursuer, now for a faster evader, and solve the game for every speed ratio $ν>1$ and every half-angle $0<α<π/2$: the escape time is characterized by explicit characteristics and the selection of roots of a scalar equation, and it is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state. Above the end $E$ of the evader's dispersal line on the front axis, the evader chases the reversing pursuer along a universal line fed by tributaries. The characteristic from the boundary of the usable part is an involute of a circle of radius $ν$ ending at a cusp, and two explicit thresholds decide whether it reaches the axis before the cusp and whether the jump of the escape time across it ends before the cusp or runs to it; in the latter case primaries fold back next to the barrier. The pursuer's optimal strategy is the relay of the slower case. The evader follows the tributaries and switches once to a primary, or commits in advance to a heading certified by the scalar equation of the primaries. Level-set and semi-Lagrangian computations are compared with the value.

Aaron D. Ames, Joe Moeller, Massimiliano de Sa, Paulo Tabuada
Layered control architectures provide a powerful paradigm for synthesizing controllers for complex systems. Yet, translating guarantees at each layer to system-level guarantees is challenging due to the interactions between layers. To address this problem, this paper presents a categorical perspective on layered control architectures. Individual systems are represented as control coalgebras, their interactions are specified as morphisms to mediators, and system-level behaviors are obtained via composition defined categorically as a pullback. To analyze the safety of these systems, we formulate control barrier morphisms (CBMs), the categorical generalization of control barrier functions. We prove that feedback controllers satisfying a CBM condition render the associated safe subobject forward invariant. It is through CBMs that we can establish the safety of layered systems: given a CBM at each layer subject to compatibility conditions, the universal property of the pullback implies the existence of a CBM for the composed system. Safety of a full-order model being safety filtered by a reduced-order model is recovered as a specialization of the categorical framework.

It builds on a variant of the primal-dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG) called reflected restarted Halpern PDHG with averaging, which we prove converges on general conic programs, and further incorporates several practical enhancements. Its GPU implementation, cuPDCS, uses customized computational schemes that assign cones of different types and sizes to different levels of the GPU architecture. Numerical experiments demonstrate that cuPDCS is generally more efficient than state-of-the-art commercial solvers and other first-order methods on large-scale conic program applications, including Fisher market equilibrium problems, Lasso regression, and multi-period portfolio optimization. cuPDCS also exhibits better scalability, efficiency, and robustness compared to other first-order methods on the conic program benchmark dataset CBLIB. These advantages are more pronounced in large-scale settings.

♻ ☆ MOE-DGSCND: Multi-Objective Enterprise Green Supply Chain Network Design
Felix Reichel
This paper introduces and studies the Multi-Objective Enterprise Doubly-Green Supply Chain Network Design (MOE-DGSCND) problem, an extension of Multi-Objective Supply Chain Network Design. The problem studied here is a three-objective combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously minimizes total cost f1, carbon dioxide emissions f2 and customer dissatisfaction f3 over binary decisions regarding which distribution centers to open and how to assign customer zones to open facilities. The problem generalizes the capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) and is known to be NP-hard (Garey and Johnson, 1979). This paper formally specifies the decision variables, objective functions and constraints and investigates three solution approaches using a single numerical instance: (A) an exact weighted-sum integer linear programming (ILP) formulation solved with Python combinatorially and via PuLP, (B) three Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes (FPTAS) providing (1 + $ε$)-approximate solutions for $ε$ := 0.15 and (C) two baseline heuristics for comparison. On an instance with eight customers and five candidate distribution centers, the exact solver certifies the optimal (sampled) supported solutions across eight weight combinations, while the FPTAS-based approaches complete within milliseconds, compared to centiseconds for the exact ILP on this tiny non-stochastic instance.

♻ ☆ Sharpness of Minima in Deep Matrix Factorization
Anil Kamber, Rahul Parhi
Understanding the loss-landscape geometry near a minimum is key to explaining the implicit bias of gradient-based methods in non-convex optimization problems such as deep neural network training and deep matrix factorization. A central quantity for characterizing this geometry is the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian of the loss. Currently, its precise role has been obfuscated because no exact expressions for this sharpness measure were known in general settings. In this paper, we present the first exact expression for the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian of the squared-error loss at any minimizer in deep matrix factorization problems, resolving an open question posed by Mulayoff and Michaeli [2020]. This expression reveals a fundamental property of the loss landscape in deep matrix factorization: It is sufficient, but not necessary, for flatness that, across all layers, the product of the spectral norms of the left and right intermediate factors equals a constant determined by the depth and the spectral norm of the target matrix. Most notably, in both depth-2 matrix factorization and deep overparameterized scalar factorization, we show that this condition is both necessary and sufficient for flatness, which implies that flat minima are spectral-norm balanced and not necessarily balanced in depth-2 matrix factorization. To complement our theory, we provide empirical verification, relying on our exact expression, of an escape phenomenon during gradient-based training near a minimizer of a deep matrix factorization problem.

♻ ☆ A Spectral Perspective on Stochastic Control Barrier Functions
Inkyu Jang, Chams E. Mballo, Claire J. Tomlin, H. Jin Kim
Stochastic control barrier functions (SCBFs) provide a safety-critical control framework for systems subject to stochastic disturbances by bounding the probability of remaining within a safe set. However, finding a valid SCBF that explicitly reflects the long-horizon behavior of the true safety probability remains a challenge. This paper addresses this issue by adopting a spectral perspective, utilizing the linear operator that governs the evolution of the closed-loop system's safety probability. We find that the dominant eigenpair of this Koopman-like operator encodes fundamental safety information of the stochastic system. The dominant eigenfunction is a natural and valid SCBF, with values that characterize relative asymptotic safety across initial states, while the dominant eigenvalue indicates the global asymptotic rate at which the safety probability decays. A practical algorithm for computation is proposed, termed power-policy iteration, which jointly estimates the dominant eigenpair while updating the backup policy with the aim of improving long-term safety. The method is validated using simulation experiments on safety-critical dynamics models.

♻ ☆ Activate the Dual Cones: A Tight Reformulation of Conic ACOPF Constraints
Saba Rafiei, Samuel Chevalier
By exploiting the observed tightness of dual rotated second-order cone (RSOC) constraints, this paper transforms the dual of a conic ACOPF relaxation into an equivalent, non-conic problem where dual constraints are implicitly enforced through eliminated dual RSOC variables. To accomplish this, we apply the RSOC-based Jabr relaxation of ACOPF, pose its dual, and then show that all dual RSOC constraints must be tight (i.e., active) at optimality. We then construct a reduced dual maximization problem with only non-negativity constraints, avoiding the explicit RSOC inequality constraints. Numerical experiments confirm that the tight formulation recovers the same dual objective values as a mature conic solver (e.g., MOSEK via PowerModels) on various PGLib benchmark test systems (ranging from 3- to 1354-buses). The proposed formulation has useful performance benefits, compared with its conic counterpart, and it allows us to define a bounding function which provides a guaranteed lower bound on system cost. While this paper focuses on demonstrating the correctness and validity of the proposed structural simplification, it lays the groundwork for future GPU-accelerated first-order optimization methods which can exploit the unconstrained nature of the proposed formulation.

We (the author and the AI systems that did the heavy lifting) show that the quantum query complexity of minimizing a convex function over a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with evaluation and membership queries is $\tildeΩ(n)$, nearly matching the best known upper bound. In particular, we show this even for quadratic minimization, which is equivalent to inverting an $n \times n$ real matrix using matrix-vector queries. We also show linear or nearly linear lower bounds on the quantum query complexity of computing the trace, the sign of the determinant, and the magnitude of the determinant of a real matrix in the matrix-vector query model. We use a novel quantum lower bound technique, the determinantal witness method, based on identifying a witness whose Fourier transform vanishes on low-rank matrices and that correlates well with the function being computed.

♻ ☆ One Model, Two Roles: Emergent Specialization in a Shared Recurrent Transformer NeurIPS 2026
Jucheng Shen, Barbara Su, Anastasios Kyrillidis
Can a shared-weight recurrent Transformer---one that repeatedly applies the same Transformer to update evolving latent states---develop distinct internal roles without being partitioned into separate modules? We study this in Asymmetric Input Recurrence (AIR), a minimal two-state reasoning architecture in which the same Transformer model is reused for both updates (per literature, L and H) and the only built-in difference in the update rule is that the encoded input is injected during L-updates but not H-updates. Across Sudoku-Extreme and Maze, decoded rollouts reveal a consistent split: $z_H$ behaves like a fully committed proposal state, whereas $z_L$ retains local uncertainty and shifting intermediate structure. Freeze interventions provide evidence of dynamical dependence between the two states, with responses that vary across tasks, intervention directions, and seeds. Ablations show that to induce specialization, the shared model needs to be able to tell the two update types apart, either from input injection asymmetry or from a separate level token. Mechanistically, attention analysis shows that L-updates are consistently more local than H-updates in both Sudoku and Maze. Together, these results show that, in a two-state recurrent setting, a clear state-identity signal can induce stable, related functional roles inside a shared-parameter recurrent Transformer. Code is available at https://github.com/juchengshen/air.

♻ ☆ Mixed-Precision GPU Acceleration for Large-Scale Minimum Enclosing Ball Problems
Ling Liang, Lei Yang
A mixed-precision GPU-oriented optimization framework is developed for computing the minimum enclosing ball of a collection of balls. The approach is built on an equivalent second-order cone programming reformulation and a relative-type inexact proximal augmented Lagrangian method (ripALM), which provides a high-accuracy optimization backbone while solving the inner subproblems only to a progress-dependent relative accuracy. The proximal augmented Lagrangian inherits a constraint-wise separable structure: its objective, gradient, generalized Hessian, and multiplier updates can be efficiently evaluated on GPUs as parallel maps over the input balls followed by reductions. To further improve efficiency, a mixed-precision reduction strategy is introduced. A low-precision ripALM run identifies balls near the approximate boundary, a high-precision ripALM run refines the reduced problem, and a full a posteriori feasibility check detects and reintroduces any violated discarded balls. Thus, low precision is used only for screening and warm starting, while the final feasibility is enforced against the original problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-data instances show that the proposed methods can compute accurate solutions, with GPU execution providing substantial speedups and mixed-precision reduction further reducing running times on most tested instances.

♻ ☆ Branch and Price for Railway Crew Scheduling: Benchmark Instances and Computational Study
Bart van Rossum
Railway crew scheduling consists of assigning a set of tasks to crew members in the form of feasible duties so as to minimise costs, and is one of the key planning problems faced by railway operators. While column generation is the dominant solution method, literature on exact branch-and-price approaches is scarce. Moreover, few publicly available benchmark instances exist. We conduct a systematic computational study of branch and price for railway crew scheduling, evaluating the contribution of branching rules, primal heuristics, and reduced cost fixing. To this end, we introduce a novel library of 100 benchmark instances, ranging in size from 90 to 3,016 tasks, each provided in a single-depot and a multi-depot variant. The instances are generated by mimicking the railway planning process, validated against data from Netherlands Railways, and publicly available with best known solutions and a solution checker. We report average optimality gaps below 1% across all instance sizes, driven primarily by the strong performance of primal heuristics, whereas branching and reduced cost fixing contribute little to closing the gap. Branch and price also outperforms a multi-commodity flow formulation, which fails to find a feasible solution on many of the smallest instances. Our findings provide support for the popularity of column generation-based primal heuristics, and show that improving the dual bound remains the main challenge for exact methods in railway crew scheduling.

Under standard nondegeneracy conditions, the active-set estimate identifies, within finite time, all constraints active at the limit point of the incumbents. Experiments on CUTEst problems show that our method generates feasible trial points more often than a comparable SQP-based approach and is competitive with an appropriate comparator in budgeted settings.

♻ ☆ From Barren Plateaus to SPSA Optimization in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
Zhen Qin
The barren plateau (BP) phenomenon poses a fundamental challenge to the trainability of variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) by causing exponentially vanishing gradients as the system size increases. While extensive studies have investigated the geometric origins of BP, its impact on the optimization dynamics and complexity of practical algorithms under finite-shot measurements has received comparatively less attention. In this paper, we develop a theoretical framework that characterizes how the BP affects the optimization dynamics of the Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) algorithm and quantifies the resulting iteration complexity and measurement budget. We derive non-asymptotic bias and variance bounds for the SPSA gradient estimator, introduce a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) defined as the ratio of the gradient energy to the mean squared error of the estimator, and establish convergence guarantees for SPSA under finite-shot measurements. Our results show that, under the proposed parameter schedules, the number of iterations sufficient to guarantee a fixed relative first-order stationarity level scales polynomially with the inverse of the intrinsic gradient energy. Consequently, when this energy decays exponentially under BP, the resulting guaranteed iteration complexity and total measurement budget both grow exponentially with the number of qubits.

In particular, we show that asymptotic and exponential stability coincide for this class. Furthermore, we introduce the real and complex stability radii for which we give explicit formulas. In addition, we consider the dual system and its application to controllability and observability. Our main results are illustrated with two examples.

We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. As a consequence, we obtain improved iteration complexity for underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo relative to overdamped Langevin methods in regimes where $\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{H})\ll d$.

Compared with reachability-analysis methods, RDDP retains the reachability mechanism while replacing local maximum-control propagation with value-function-guided control selection, thereby enabling objectives beyond traversal time. The approximate policy is shown to outperform benchmark decision rules mirroring real-world assignment strategies. Further numerical experiments are conducted to analyze different operational policies: (1) inclusion of overtime drivers in the reserve operator roster; (2) reward weights for work tasks that consider passenger wait time saved. Observations from these computational analyses provide actionable insights into extraboard sizing, overtime usage, and real-time dispatch practices at transit agencies.

April Niu, Santanu Dey, Oktay Günlük, Jisun Lee
We study the \textit{Boxing Problem}, which seeks a subset of points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) maximizing the total reward of a selection of points minus the width of its axis-aligned bounding box. After anchoring, we establish a connection to the intersection of mixing sets with a linking constraint, which yields a polynomial-time optimization algorithm and a polynomial-size extended formulation. Under severe capacity scarcity, congestion remains relevant at the classical Dorfman scale: the square-root law survives, but with a capacity-dependent constant. Dynamic pooling separates two operational decisions that fixed pool sizes conflate. A lower threshold determines when routine testing should begin, while an upper threshold limits pooling when backlog is high. The lower threshold follows the cube-root scale, whereas the upper threshold primarily acts as congestion control. The results show how prevalence, capacity, and delay jointly determine pooling decisions and explain why operationally optimal pools can be much smaller than those suggested by test-efficiency calculations alone.

The literature contains several legacy metaheuristics for the TRP; however, most are evaluated on small- and medium-scale instances and show limited scalability for large and extreme datasets. GILS-RVND, the current gold standard in metaheuristic algorithms, performs well on small and medium instances but struggles to scale due to the exhaustive neighborhood search in the RVND phase. To address this limitation, we introduce Restricted 2-Opt And Ruin-and-recreate (ROAR), a Large Neighborhood Search-based method that integrates ruin-and-recreate with greedy insertion and a restricted, insertion-anchored 2-opt operator. Computational experiments demonstrate that ROAR produces high-quality solutions for large-scale instances and outperforms existing methods under strict time limits. We further introduce an O(1)-time, O(1)-space algorithm for evaluating 2-opt moves during a contiguous systematic sweep, which, to the best of our knowledge, is unprecedented. Finally, we evaluate ROAR on instances with up to 200,000 nodes, substantially exceeding the largest instances previously reported in the literature (11,849 nodes).

☆ A Two-Stage Optimization Framework for Real-World Large-Scale University Course Timetabling Based on Orthogonalized Hierarchical Modeling and Conflict-Driven ALNS Repair
Han-Bin Liu, Huayi Wei, Yanlin Li
University course timetabling is a large-scale combinatorial optimization problem involving strongly coupled temporal and resource constraints. This paper proposes a two-stage optimization framework for real-world large-scale university course timetabling, integrating orthogonalized hierarchical modeling with conflict-driven adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) repair. The first stage performs global course-level optimization, while the second identifies residual conflicts through a conflict graph and localizes them into connected conflict regions. The Course--Occurrence--Session representation provides the structural basis for multi-granularity repair, which employs Cluster-, Course-, Occurrence-, and Session-level destroy operators within the ALNS framework, followed by fine-grained greedy repair. The framework is evaluated on a real-world university timetabling instance involving 3,073 course groups, 8,015 scheduling events, 998 student classes, and 1,511 instructors. Ablation experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of hierarchical repair granularity and adaptive operator selection. Across ten independent runs, the ALNS + Greedy framework achieves a mean residual conflict count of 18.50, compared with 172 for deterministic Greedy-only repair under the same initial scheduling conditions, representing an 89.24\% reduction. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed conflict-driven hierarchical repair framework for large-scale university course timetabling.

We investigate observer-based event-triggered stabilization of infinite-dimensional linear systems, such as those governed by partial differential equations. A Luenberger observer and a feedback gain are assumed to stabilize the closed loop in continuous time, and we study what happens when the control input is only updated at instants generated by a dynamic event-triggering mechanism. Unlike approaches that rely on state-dependent triggering rules, our condition only involves the observer state and the measured output, which makes it implementable when the full state is not measured. It compares the deviation of a monitored signal of the observer since the last update with a threshold made of two parts. The first one is a relative part, proportional to the current size of this signal, and the second one is a positive internal variable, which does not depend on the observer state. In particular, the case where the threshold reduces to the internal variable alone is covered. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the well-posedness of the closed-loop system and the absence of Zeno behavior for general choices of these two parts, and we prove its exponential stability under a small-gain condition on the relative part. We further analyse the existence of a dwell-time, namely a positive lower bound on the time elapsed between two consecutive triggering instants. When the sampled dynamics is bounded, as in finite-dimensional systems or systems with a finite-dimensional unstable part, we obtain a dwell-time independent of the initial data, together with exponential stability. For unbounded generators, we exhibit a system satisfying all our assumptions for which no triggering rule can achieve both a dwell-time independent of the initial data and bounded trajectories.

Global supply chains are increasingly exposed to trade policy shocks and physical disruptions arising from common geopolitical events. We develop a robust optimization framework with two decision stages for strategic supply chain reconfiguration. Supplier qualification and transportation arc activation decisions are made before uncertainty is realized, while operational flows adapt afterward. Geopolitical uncertainty is represented through country level shocks that can jointly trigger tariff escalation, policy induced restrictions on cross border capacity, facility disruptions, and physical transportation failures. The resulting min max min problem is reformulated by dualizing the operational recourse problem, yielding a nonconvex mixed integer bilinear adversarial problem solved within a column and constraint generation procedure. Comparison with complete enumeration verifies the implementation on small instances, while experiments on 60 synthetic supply chain networks of varying sizes assess computational performance. The results show that omitting geopolitical transmission channels during strategic design can lead to substantial deterioration in cost and service under full geopolitical stress. Broader protection is achieved primarily through changes in transportation network configuration rather than increased supplier qualification. Robust performance also depends on the severity and composition of geopolitical consequences, with restrictions on cross border capacity exerting a stronger effect than comparable proportional changes in tariff severity over the tested ranges. A geographically grounded case analysis further shows that the value of individual uncertainty channels depends on network structure and geographic exposure.

To block it, a barrier can be constructed in real time, at speed $λ>0$. A long standing conjecture by the first author states that the fire can be entirely surrounded by the barrier, in finite time, if and only if $λ>2$. The present paper improves on earlier lower bounds. Namely, if $λ\leq Λ=1.62621170228\ldots $ we show that the fire cannot be blocked. We also prove that, if $λ\leq 2$, the fire cannot be blocked by constructing a barrier which is a simple closed curve. More precisely, if the barrier does not contain purely delaying arcs, i.e.~arcs which are eventually surrounded by the fire on both sides, then for $λ<2$ the region burned by the fire at time $t>0$ has area $A(t)>(2-λ)t^2/4$.

In this work, we implement and compare three formulations equally across a diverse set of instances. We extend these three representations to handle heterogeneous cargo in terms of size and weight, and to address advanced stability requirements, such as centre of gravity limits, stress force limits, and ballast-water adjustments. The hybrid-slot and grid-based models both perform well finding solutions for 447 out of 486 instances across all configurations; however, the hybrid-slot model placed 8% more cargo than the grid model. By contrast, the lane model only finds solutions for 142 instances and placed 15% less cargo than the grid-based model. The solutions generated by the hybrid-slot model are validated using a commercial vessel-stability software to verify our stability estimations, showing issues in only 24 of 162 instances, which are easily avoided by tightening the stability constraints. Finally, we address the placement of hazardous and refrigerated cargo in an efficient manner for the hybrid-slot model by employing lazy constraints which is shown to solve realistic sized instances.

These hardness results hold regardless of whether the input constraint set is given in H- or V-representation.

Specifically, under mild assumptions on the estimated parameters, we develop a unified error analysis that incorporates both sources of error, and establish the relevant convergence rates for the computational efficiency loss. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. Mateo Díaz, Nicolás García Trillos, Daniel López-Castaño, Congwei Yang
Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. This behavior is in contrast with SignSGD which has no transition, leading to different optimal learning rates, but with matching convergence rate up to a constant factor in the isotropic setting. For anisotropic data, large batch setting Muon performs a square-root preconditioning with respect to the data covariance spectrum while SignSGD provides no preconditioning for generic covariances. We analyze time to target loss in a power law covariance model and derive a phase diagram in the data exponent $α$ and target exponent $ζ$. Muon is favored for steep covariance spectra with rich targets ($α>2$, $ζ<α+1$), SignSGD is favored for flat spectra ($α<1$), and in other regions the winner depends on how the target loss scales with dimension. Our results shed light on why replacing Adam with Muon is not trivial even from a pure optimization perspective.

When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.
♻ ☆ Equilibrium Singular Dividend Control with Regime Switching and Bankruptcy under Non-Exponential Discounting
Xiaochen Chen, Guohui Guan, Zongxia Liang, Xiaodong Luo
This paper studies an infinite-horizon equilibrium dividend problem for a firm whose surplus follows a diffusion with observable Markov regime switching and is absorbed at bankruptcy. Dividend payments are modeled as singular controls, and non-exponential discounting gives rise to time inconsistency. We formulate equilibrium control laws and establish a verification theorem for a general finite-state model with surplus-dependent coefficients. For a two-state model with constant positive drifts and volatilities and bi-exponential discounting, we prove the existence of a regime-dependent equilibrium barrier strategy for arbitrary positive switching intensities. The proof relies on uniform estimates for a system of coupled boundary-value problems and the Poincaré-Miranda theorem. We also verify that the resulting strategy satisfies the equilibrium variational inequalities. Numerical results show that greater dispersion in discount rates, with the initial average discount rate held fixed, raises both barriers. The effect of switching intensity can be nonmonotone and may reverse the ordering of the barriers.
♻ ☆ From Global Optimization to Exact Coordinates: Heilbronn's Triangle Problem on the Unit Square Using Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Optimization
Nathan Sudermann-Merx
We develop a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) approach for the Heilbronn triangle problem on the unit square. The formulation exploits the boundary structure of optimal configurations, which we establish rigorously, to fix coordinates and orientation variables a priori. With this formulation, a general-purpose global solver solves the case $n=9$ to global optimality within its numerical tolerances in about eight minutes on a laptop and without any precomputation, compared with about 23 hours of total computation for the best previous approach. The same model also solves $n=10$ for the first time, in under seven hours, and confirms the configuration of Comellas and Yebra (2002). The numerical solutions then guide an exact symbolic reconstruction, and the minimum triangle area of every reconstructed configuration is verified in exact arithmetic. This yields exact coordinates for all $n\le 10$, including the configurations of Comellas and Yebra (2002) for $n=9$ and $n=10$, together with rigorous lower bounds. Finally, we derive structural properties of optimal configurations, formulate a conjecture on the number of critical triangles, and pose an open question. All code and data are publicly available.

♻ ☆ It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity and Limits of Continuous Encoders for Over-the-Air Computation
Saeed Razavikia
We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.
♻ ☆ A model predictive control framework with robust stability guarantees under unbounded disturbances
Johannes Köhler, Melanie N. Zeilinger
To address feasibility issues in model predictive control (MPC), most implementations relax state constraints by using slack variables and adding a penalty to the cost. We propose an alternative strategy: relaxing the initial state constraint with a penalty. Compared to state-of-the-art soft constrained MPC formulations, the proposed formulation has two key features: (i) input-to-state stability and bounds on the cumulative constraint violation for unbounded disturbances; (ii) close-to-optimal performance under nominal operating conditions. The idea is initially presented for open-loop asymptotically stable nonlinear systems by designing the penalty as a Lyapunov function, but we also show how to relax this condition to: i) Lyapunov stable systems; ii) stabilizable systems; and iii) utilizing an implicit characterization of the Lyapunov function. In the special case of linear systems, the proposed MPC formulation reduces to a quadratic program, and the offline design and online computational complexity are only marginally increased compared to a nominal design. Numerical examples demonstrate benefits compared to state-of-the-art soft-constrained MPC formulations.
comment: Extended version of accepted paper in Automatica. Appendix contains additional details
♻ ☆ A derivative-free trust-region approach for Low Order-Value Optimization problems
Anderson E. Schwertner, Francisco N. C. Sobral
The Low Order-Value Optimization (LOVO) problem involves minimizing the minimum among a finite number of function values within a feasible set. LOVO has several practical applications such as robust parameter estimation, protein alignment, portfolio optimization, among others. In this work, we are interested in the constrained nonlinear optimization LOVO problem of minimizing the minimum between a finite number of function values subject to a nonempty closed convex set where each function is a black-box and continuously differentiable, but the derivatives are not available. We develop the first derivative-free trust-region algorithm for constrained LOVO problems with convergence to weakly critical points. Under suitable conditions, we establish the global convergence of the algorithm and also its worst-case iteration complexity analysis. An initial open-source implementation using only linear interpolation models is developed. Extensive numerical experiments and comparison with existing alternatives show the properties and the efficiency of the proposed approach when solving LOVO problems.
♻ ☆ Logic-Based Benders Decomposition for Time Slot Management with Mixed Logit Demand
Dorsa Abdolhamidi, Carla Juvin, Virginie Lurkin
This paper develops an exact solution framework for the choice-based time slot management problem under mixed logit demand in attended home delivery systems. The problem jointly optimizes delivery slot offerings, price discounts, and routing decisions, with customer choices endogenously modeled through a simulation-based mixed logit formulation embedded via sample average approximation, resulting in a large-scale stochastic mixed-integer program. To address this complexity, we propose a logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) that separates strategic assortment and pricing decisions, together with customer choice, from scenario-specific vehicle routing subproblems. We derive problem-specific optimality cuts that exploit the routing structure to provide stronger bounds than generic cuts, and establish their validity. To enhance computational performance, we introduce and systematically evaluate several strengthening strategies, including relaxation-based cut generation and capacity- and flow-based valid inequalities. We further compare two equivalent encodings of the embedded choice model and show that the relative value of each strengthening strategy depends on the strength of the master formulation it complements. Computational experiments on benchmark instances show that the proposed framework significantly extends the range of solvable instances compared to direct MILP approaches. The framework is exact: it converges to a proven optimal solution given sufficient time, and the bounds it produces at intermediate iterations are valid. Within a 12-hour limit, proven optimality is reached for instances with up to 10 customers, and valid bounds are obtained up to 40 customers, including sizes at which the direct MILP formulation returns no feasible solution.
♻ ☆ A Search-Based Algorithm for Multistage Robust Discrete Linear Optimization and its Implementation
Michael Hartisch, Ulf Lorenz
Robust optimization models that allow decisions to adapt to newly revealed information remain computationally challenging and are often limited to two decision stages or are addressed heuristically or via approximation schemes. This challenge is further amplified when uncertainty sets depend on earlier decisions. Conventional approaches to such problems often require problem-specific reformulations and tailored algorithms, highlighting the need for an exact model-and-run approach. We address this gap by presenting an algorithmic framework for solving multistage robust discrete linear optimization problems. This exact approach adapts and integrates ideas from game-tree search, quantified conflict-driven clause learning, and integer linear programming to explore the minimax tree and is implemented in the open-source solver Yasol. The solver supports discrete decision variables across multiple stages, discrete uncertainty sets with polyhedral or decision-dependent structure, and mixed-integer recourse in the final stage. It can be used as a standalone executable or through a C++ library interface, allowing it to serve as a reference solver for exact methods in multistage robust discrete linear optimization. In an extensive computational study, we demonstrate the capabilities of our solver. The results show competitive performance against a reference approach from the literature for a protection-interdiction problem, as well as strong performance on bilevel benchmark instances. For a multistage cutting-stock problem, we demonstrate the substantial loss in solution quality that can arise from neglecting the multistage structure and show that our solver significantly outperforms decision-rule approximations in terms of computational efficiency while certifying the true multistage optimum.
♻ ☆ Theoretical and Computational Advances in Birkhoff Pseudospectral Transcription for Aerospace Optimal Control

Birkhoff pseudospectral methods replace the differentiation matrices of classical transcriptions with integration operators whose conditioning does not deteriorate with polynomial order. This paper presents theoretical and computational advancements toward their practical use in aerospace optimal control. The initial-point-anchored Birkhoff integration operator is constructed explicitly for flipped Legendre-Gauss-Radau grids and related exactly to the corresponding Lagrange differentiation matrix and, through a reflection, to the standard Radau Birkhoff operator, whose conditioning properties it inherits. Rate constraints on nonlinear functions of states and controls are enforced directly through the pseudospectral operators and, for control-rate limits, shown to be primal and dual equivalent to state augmentation. Non-affine time mappings concentrate the nodes around localized trajectory features, and composing affine scaling and equilibration transformations provides a systematic way to construct scaling strategies. The methods are implemented in the open-source MATLAB framework RAPTOR and tested across a range of challenging optimal control problems, including a dense-grid orbit-raising problem, a rate-limited landing scenario, a Space Shuttle entry problem, and a five-phase reusable-launch-vehicle mission.
♻ ☆ Conditional Sampling via Wasserstein Autoencoders and Triangular Transport
Mohammad Al-Jarrah, Michele Martino, Marcus Yim, Bamdad Hosseini, Amirhossein Taghvaei
We present Conditional Wasserstein Autoencoders (CWAEs), a framework for conditional simulation that exploits low-dimensional structure in both the conditioned and the conditioning variables. The key idea is to modify a Wasserstein autoencoder to use a (block-) triangular decoder and impose an appropriate independence assumption on the latent variables. We show that the resulting model gives an autoencoder that can exploit low-dimensional structure while simultaneously the decoder can be used for conditional simulation. We explore various theoretical properties of CWAEs, including their connections to conditional optimal transport (OT) problems. We also present alternative formulations that lead to three architectural variants forming the foundation of our algorithms. We present a series of numerical experiments that demonstrate that our different CWAE variants achieve substantial reductions in approximation error relative to the low-rank ensemble Kalman filter (LREnKF), particularly in problems where the support of the conditional measures is truly low-dimensional.
