We study online learning in linear dynamical games where multiple strategic agents act on a shared state evolving according to a linear dynamical system subject to adversarial disturbances. This setting lies beyond both single-agent nonstochastic online control and classical linear-quadratic games, which typically focus on quadratic objectives and noiseless or stochastic dynamics. Each agent seeks to minimize its own sequence of convex losses under full-state observability. Following the stabilizing-baseline paradigm in nonstochastic online control, we assume access to linear controllers that stabilize the noiseless system and focus on online adaptation by learning disturbance-action corrections. This extends adversarial online control to strategic multi-agent shared-state systems, where each agent's actions shape the state trajectory and hence the realized losses of all learners. Under state-only and aggregate-input feedback models, we analyze agents running online gradient descent with memory to update their own disturbance-action policies. We prove per-agent regret bounds that are sublinear and near-optimal in the time horizon, with population dependence that varies under the specified feedback, opponent policy, and stability assumptions. In the common-interest case, where all agents have identical cost functions, we show that the induced online problem forms a time-varying potential game and derive equilibrium tracking guarantees. Together, our results provide a theoretical framework for adversarial online learning in stabilized linear dynamical games, connecting online control with learning in games.

The objective function for this category is characterized by the ratio of a numerator and denominator, both being convex, semi-algebraic and differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradients over the constraint sets. The constrained sets associated with these problems are closed, convex, and semi-algebraic. We propose an efficient algorithm that is inspired by the proximal gradient method, and we provide a thorough convergence analysis. Our algorithm is shown to converge to a critical point without the typical need for a nonnegative numerator, and this critical point becomes a globally optimal solution whenever the numerator is nonpositive at the initial point. Our approach is adaptable to unbounded constraint sets as well. Therefore, our approach is viable for many more practical models. Numerical experiments show that our method not only reliably reaches ground-truth solutions in some model problems but also outperforms several existing methods in maximizing the Sharpe ratio with real-world financial data.

When the objective function is convex and the Lagrangian satisfies the Flatness condition, an appropriate parameter choice yields a worst-case convergence rate of O(1/t^2). Furthermore, incorporating the Growth condition guarantees this worst-case rate of O(1/t^2) for any function satisfying these assumptions if and only if the parameter is chosen above a suitable threshold; under this condition, even faster convergence can be achieved. For the algorithmic construction, a numerical scheme is derived by discretizing the proposed ODE. We also investigate the influence of algorithm parameters and provide insights into their optimal selection. As a workaround, reduced-order models (ROMs) are often employed, which replace the full PDE system and alleviate the computational burden while solving optimal control problems. However, when the underlying PDE exhibits transport-dominated behavior, standard reduced-order modeling techniques like proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) that rely on linear approximation spaces may require a large number of modes due to the slowly decaying Kolmogorov $n$-width. To overcome this challenge, we focus on the use of transformed POD as a reduced-order model, which is particularly effective in capturing low-dimensional representations of high-fidelity transport-dominated phenomena. In this work, a reduced-order model is constructed first, followed by the optimization of the reduced system. For linear systems generated by strongly continuous groups, we prove existence and uniqueness of solutions for the ROM under an explicit smallness condition on the control, as well as the existence of an optimal control for sufficiently large regularization. The numerical experiments concern the 1D linear advection equation with a subset of the general transformation groups called the shift transformations. Additionally, we compare the computational performance of the shifted POD (sPOD) method against the standard POD.
♻ ☆ Proximal Limited-Memory Quasi-Newton Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization
Simeon vom Dahl, Alberto De Marchi, Christian Kanzow
We propose a regularized proximal quasi-Newton method (RPQN) for minimizing the sum of a continuously differentiable, possibly nonconvex function and a proper, lower semicontinuous, prox-bounded, possibly nonconvex regularizer. The method uses adaptive quadratic regularization and limited-memory quasi-Newton models. We establish global convergence under weak assumptions, without requiring global Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, and prove convergence of the entire sequence, with rates, under the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property. To solve the proximal subproblems efficiently, we exploit compact limited-memory representations and derive a compact representation of the Kleinmichel rank-one update, which preserves positive definiteness under the same condition as BFGS. Numerical experiments on logistic and Student's regression demonstrate competitive performance and the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
comment: 30 pages
♻ ☆ American Options with Last Exit Times: A Free-Boundary Approach
Zhuoshu Wu, Libo Li
We study an optimal stopping problem with a random horizon that is not a stopping time: the last exit time of a geometric Brownian motion from a fixed level $L$. The defaultable American put option serves as the motivating example. Using the theory of enlargements of filtration and the associated Azéma supermartingale, we reduce the problem to a classical optimal stopping problem in a finite time horizon for a Markov process, whose gain function is only upper semi-continuous and has a concave kink at $L$ and a spatial derivative that blows up. These features break the standard free-boundary arguments, including the smooth-fit condition. We describe the continuation and stopping sets according to the position of $L$ relative to $B$, the optimal stopping boundary of the standard American put option. When $B$ lies completely above $L$, the random-horizon problem coincides with the standard American put option pricing problem on the continuation set. When $B$ lies below $L$ for some time interval, the optimal stopping boundary of the random-horizon problem lies below or stays at $L$ until $B$ reaches $L$ and agrees with $B$ when $B$ exceeds $L$. The smooth-fit condition fails at $L$, and we obtain upper and lower bounds for the one-sided derivative of the value function. Under numerically verifiable parameter conditions, we show that the boundary is monotone and continuous, and we derive a nonlinear integral equation and an early-exercise-premium representation with local time terms.
♻ ☆ The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures
Thomas Schmelzer, Trevor Hastie
Many statistical procedures compute an entire solution path rather than a single estimator. For one class the path is piecewise linear, traced corner to corner by an active-set homotopy. Two of its members coincide exactly: under $Σ=X^\top X$ and $μ=X^\top y$ the gross-exposure-constrained mean--variance program and the constrained LASSO trace the same piecewise-linear curve, and they keep doing so under arbitrary linear equality and inequality constraints. Which parameter is swept, a leverage budget or a return tilt, is not a choice the curve notices: under a homogeneous mandate the two sweeps differ by a scalar. A mandate that holds the portfolio invested costs a radial rescaling instead, and the efficient frontier is that curve rescaled; its corners pass unnoticed because the frontier is continuously differentiable where they fall. We give the map between the two parametrisations and the single way it degenerates. That mean--variance selection and the LASSO instantiate one parametric quadratic program is prior art (Gärtner, Jaggi and Maria, 2012). The Critical Line Algorithm itself lies off that route, and the correspondence established here is new. The identity is one of curves, not of statistical experiments. The map between the parametrisations is computed from the data, so the geometry of the path transfers while quantities averaged over the response do not. We cross that boundary deliberately and give the degrees of freedom of the constrained fit under arbitrary linear constraints. In the long-only, fully invested case it is the expected number of holdings away from a bound, less one.

♻ ☆ Geometry-Dependent Approximation for Non-Monotone $k$-Submodular Maximization
Vaneet Aggarwal
We study the maximization of a nonnegative $k$-submodular function, not assumed monotone, in which each of $n$ elements receives one of $k\ge2$ labels or stays unselected and the selected elements must satisfy a constraint. For a compact convex down-closed region $P\subseteq[0,1]^n$ of fractional selection vectors, the diagonal level $ζ(P)=\max\{t\in[0,1]:t(1,\ldots,1)\in P\}$ is the largest selection probability that can be given to all elements at once; it equals $r/n$ for a uniform matroid of rank $r$, and $ζ(P)=1$ means that the constraint is vacuous. We give approximation coefficients that increase continuously with $ζ$. They come from one inequality for the multilinear extension of the objective: the algorithm computes an action without querying the objective, and objective feedback gives a comparator-independent update direction. For $k\ge3$, feasibility of the action reduces to three polynomial inequalities in one variable; for $k=2$ the profile is closed form. At $ζ=0$ the coefficients are $0.4456\ldots$ for $k=2$ and $0.4541\ldots$ for every $k\ge3$. For every finite $k\ge3$ they reach $1/2$ above an explicit level, which is $0.4026\ldots$ for $k=3,4,5$, and at $ζ=1$ they reach $1/2$ for $k=2$, $(\sqrt{17}-3)/2$ for $k=3,4$, and $k/(2k-1)$ for $k\ge5$. Online linear optimization gives $O(\sqrt T)$ approximate regret, with gradient feedback or with value queries made after each action. The coefficients carry over to matroids, with expected and high-probability guarantees, and to any fixed number of knapsacks: the zero-level coefficients hold on every instance, and the larger ones when items are small or when prefix enumeration keeps the diagonal level on one branch. For one budget the enumeration exponent is $O(1/\varepsilon)$.

☆ EnerGNN: Learning Optimization-Compatible Energy Functions for Exact Constrained Combinatorial Inference NeurIPS 2026
Niki Triantafyllou, Maria M. Papathanasiou
Learning-based approaches to combinatorial optimization often predict solutions directly or use predictions to restrict search, while expressive energy-based models typically rely on approximate inference. We introduce EnerGNN, a framework that learns energy functions over complete binary configurations and minimizes them under explicit hard constraints through mixed integer programming (MIP). EnerGNN combines a graph neural network encoder with an optimization-compatible readout and a nonlinear energy head, enabling exact constrained inference over the learned energy. An optimality-aware contrastive loss trains the energy to reflect solution quality and constraint violations. Across Quadratic Knapsack, Combinatorial Auctions, and a personalized cell therapy supply chain problem, EnerGNN achieves near-optimal solutions with 100% feasibility. On the supply chain problem, it achieves a 0.05% mean primal gap and a 17.4$\times$ speedup over the monolithic MIP. The learned energy also generalizes to larger instances and supports zero-shot constraint injection, adapting to changing constraints without retraining while preserving feasibility.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
☆ Minimum-coordinate elimination on a simplex: polynomial first-step safety and coNP-complete correctness
Arseny Kosachev
We study a deletion rule for strictly convex quadratic minimization on a simplex: compute the affine minimizer on the current face, permanently remove a most-negative coordinate, and repeat. Correctness is required for every linear term and every resolution of ties. We characterize first-step safety by a finite maximum principle for the constrained inverse, and correctness from every initial face by principal-inverse row inequalities. Correctness from the full simplex is a different property. The two properties coincide with at most four coordinates, but an explicit rational five-coordinate example separates them. An exact reachability condition explains the separation: boundary equalities in the constrained inverse restrict the tasks that can be entered on a facet. Away from these equalities, full-start and hereditary correctness coincide. We also determine the recognition complexity. First-step safety is decidable in polynomial bit time, by combining classical strict $n$-step-vector recognition with diagonal regularization. In contrast, full-start and hereditary correctness are coNP-complete, even on a reduction family with strict column diagonal maxima on every face. The proofs include the non-strict boundary and all affine anchors; explicit rational certificates for the finite examples are given in the text.
comment: 25 pages
☆ Ellipsoid Separation in Data-Dependent Time via Infimal Displacement Vectors
Matthew Hough, Stephen A. Vavasis
The infimal displacement vector of the nonexpansive operator underlying the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm (PDHG) is known to encode useful information for infeasible optimization problems. In particular, for the ellipsoid separation problem (ESP), where the goal is to find a separating hyperplane between two collections of ellipsoids, the infimal displacement vector corresponding to an infeasible second-order cone program (SOCP) encodes a separating hyperplane. We show FISTA computes a sequence of approximations to the dual component of the infimal displacement vector and establish that a solution to the ESP can be obtained in $\mathcal{O}(δ_{\mathcal{A}}^{-2})$ iterations. Here $δ_{\mathcal{A}}$ denotes the distance between the convex hulls of the two ellipsoid collections.
☆ Using artificial delays for prescribed/fixed-time static output feedback control of linear systems
Kang-Kang Zhang, Emilia Fridman
In this paper, we address the prescribed/fixed-time control problem for linear time-invariant systems with relative degree $r\geq 2$ using delayed time-varying static output feedback. In addition to controllability and observability, we assume that a truncated observability matrix is nonsingular. Within the act-and-wait control framework, two types of artificial delays are introduced into the output feedback: one to realize static output feedback and the other to achieve prescribed/fixed-time control. By constructing smooth periodic delayed output feedback controllers, we achieve prescribed-time input-to-state stability (ISS) with respect to matched disturbances and measurement noise. Next, we consider systems with measurement delays. Note that existing predictor methods are not applicable to static output feedback delay compensation. We propose delayed controllers that achieve fixed-time stability in the presence of large known slowly-varying delays (with delay derivatives less than one) and even in the presence of large unknown constant delays for systems with nilpotent matrices. Moreover, we present a design for the case of discrete-time periodic measurements with a small sampling period. When the system reduces to a chain of integrators, prescribed/fixed-time convergence can be achieved with arbitrarily large artificial delays introduced by static output feedback avoiding high gain and managing with large known slowly-varying or sawtooth delays (corresponding to discrete-time measurements) or unknown constant delays. In the case of unknown constant delays, this leads to a low-gain controller that may efficiently attenuate measurement noise. Numerical examples verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures
☆ V-Representability Beyond Singular Times in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: The Hubbard Dimer Case
Éric Cancès, Théo Duez
We study the global $V$-representability problem in time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) for the two-particle Hubbard dimer model in the spin-singlet sector. In particular, we investigate whether the time-dependent density of the interacting system obtained for a given one-body external potential $u$ (the tunable control variable) can be reproduced by a non-interacting Kohn--Sham system beyond the singular times at which the usual inversion formulas break down. We deal with both the conventional formulation of TDDFT based on some time-dependent variational principle and the recently introduced geometric formulation of TDDFT (Phys. Rev. Lett. 136 (2026) 256401, Phys. Rev. A 113 (2026) 062222). For both principles, we prove global-in-time $V$-representability, show that singular times induce non-uniqueness of the time-dependent effective potential, and classify the set of solutions.
comment: 49 pages, 10 figures
☆ A Cubic Underestimator for Deterministic Global Optimization
Krishan Kumar, Ishan Bajaj
We propose a new underestimator with pointwise and Hausdorff convergence of order three for deterministic global optimization of twice continuously differentiable functions with Lipschitz continuous Hessians. The proposed underestimator is obtained by augmenting the second-order Taylor expansion with a cubic remainder term of the objective function yielding a valid global underestimator that can be used to obtain lower bounds in a branch-and-bound method to solve nonconvex global optimization problems. The underestimator is nonconvex, and finding its global minimum could be computationally expensive. Accordingly, we derive a sufficient condition under which the proposed cubic underestimator is edge-concave, so that its minimum over a box can be found by vertex evaluation, while retaining third-order convergence. We show that the maximum separation distance between the objective function and the underestimator decreases cubically with the width of the box. This higher order convergence enables the lower bounds to converge more rapidly to the optimal value as the variable bounds are progressively tightened. The proposed underestimator is incorporated into a deterministic branch-and-bound algorithm and compared with the αBB and second-order edge-concave underestimators on a collection of 130 benchmark problems. The numerical results show that the proposed underestimator outperforms the compared underestimators in terms of both the number of explored branch-and-bound nodes and total CPU time, while maintaining a competitive computational cost per node. These results demonstrate that the proposed cubic edge-concave underestimator can provide more effective lower bounds and better computational performance in deterministic global optimization.
☆ Optimal Control of the 2D Boussinesq Equations with Finite Codimension Constraints
Utpal Manna, Manil T. Mohan, Sangram Satpathi
We study an optimal control problem (OCP) governed by the two-dimensional (2D) Boussinesq equations, where the right-hand sides of the velocity and temperature equations are projected onto the corresponding tangent spaces of the manifolds $\mathcal{M}_1:=\{y\in\mathbb{H}:\|y\|_{\mathbb{H}}=1\}$ and $\mathcal{M}_2:=\{θ\in H:\|θ\|_H=1\}$, respectively. The resulting evolution is subject to finite-codimensional constraints, under which the state $(y,θ)$ remains on $\mathcal{M}:=\mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2$ throughout the time interval. A Faedo--Galerkin construction provides a unique, global, strong solution to the constrained Boussinesq system for external controls $\mathfrak{H}\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb{H})$, along with uniform energy bounds. In addition, we establish the existence of an optimal triplet $(y^*,θ^*,\mathfrak{H}^*)$ that minimizes the quadratic cost subject to the constrained Boussinesq system. Necessary conditions of the first order are obtained through a coupled state--adjoint--control system. The optimal state $(y^*,θ^*)$ remains on $\mathcal{M}$, while the optimal control lies in the tangent space: $\mathfrak{H}^*(t)\in T_{y^*(t)}\mathcal{M}_1$, for all $t\in[0,T]$. We also show that the map $\mathfrak{H}\mapsto(y_{\mathfrak{H}},θ_{\mathfrak{H}})$ in $(C([0,T];\mathbb{H})\cap L^2(0,T;\mathbb{V}))\times(C([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V))$ is Fréchet differentiable. The linearized state is the unique weak solution to the constrained linearized Boussinesq system and satisfies the necessary tangency condition. Hence, the well-posedness and first-order optimality conditions are established for the Boussinesq system under nonlinear manifold constraints.
comment: 47 pages
☆ When Protection Hurts: A Cytokine Storm Theory of Supply Chain Overreaction
Gurkirat Wadhwa
Supply chain resilience research has traditionally viewed defensive actions such as safety stock, backup suppliers, expedited transportation, and emergency sourcing as beneficial. However, disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2021 semiconductor shortage, and the Suez Canal blockage highlight how synchronized hoarding, duplicate ordering, and capacity reservation can amplify congestion and operational costs, sometimes worsening the original disruption. Motivated by this observation, we develop a decision-theoretic framework in which Protective Response Intensity (PRI) is an endogenous decision variable. We introduce Response-Induced Loss (RIL) to capture costs generated by defensive actions and characterize a unique optimal response that balances disruption mitigation against self-induced losses. We derive a closed-form critical response threshold beyond which RIL exceeds the original disruption intensity, a phenomenon termed a *Supply Chain Cytokine Storm*. We further propose the Cytokine Storm Index (CSI), measuring response-induced loss relative to the original disruption, and discuss its potential calibration using operational data. Extending the framework to interconnected supply networks, we derive a spectral stability condition distinguishing bounded decentralized responses from network-wide propagation. Numerical experiments show that optimal responses remain below the storm threshold, whereas proportional response heuristics can exceed it. Network responses converge or diverge according to the derived stability condition. Overall, our findings highlight that supply chain resilience depends not only on mitigating disruptions but also on keeping defensive responses proportionate to the shocks they are intended to address.
♻ ☆ Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport with Pearson Marginal Penalties
Minh-Nhat Phung, Minh-Binh Tran
We study quadratically regularized unbalanced optimal transport with Pearson marginal penalties and a lower bound $δ\ge0$ on the plan, including the sparse case $δ=0$. We organize the analysis around the active interface, where the plan switches from its lower bound to larger values. We prove a Newton remainder estimate that depends linearly on the marginal measure of the boundary layer around this interface, and a maximum-norm inverse estimate uniform over all Newton derivatives and cell volumes. Together they give local superlinear convergence of semismooth Newton iteration in function space, of q-order at least $1+α$ when the boundary-layer measure is $O(t^α)$, and a common convergence neighborhood along each refinement sequence whose data converge uniformly. Transverse interfaces give second-order supercloseness of the discrete potentials to the cell averages of the continuum potentials. A directional curvature condition on the input data verifies the interface condition before the solution is known and yields an explicit Newton convergence radius on all sufficiently fine meshes, uniformly in the lower bound. A globalized inexact semismooth Newton iteration has mesh-independent numbers of outer iterations and of full-array operations, that is, passes over the plan array. Its output satisfies an a posteriori error bound relative to the continuum optimal plan. Experiments test the rates at transverse interfaces and at interfaces with tangencies, the curvature criterion, and the algorithmic work. All estimates hold for a fixed regularization parameter and a fixed lower bound on the densities.

♻ ☆ On the Theory of Bias Tuning in Event Cameras
David El-Chai Ben-Ezra, Daniel Brisk, Adar Tal
This paper lays the foundation of a theory for bias tuning in neuromorphic cameras, a novel sensing technology also known as "event cameras". We begin by formulating the high-level effect of the sensitivity biases on the camera's event rate in mathematical terms. We then show that, as a corollary of the Poincare-Miranda theorem, the commonly used tuning principles of rate budgeting and polarity balancing lead to a unique configuration of the sensitivity biases. As a corollary, we show how by adopting these principles, the multi-variable bias-tuning problem reduces to a two-parameter problem that can be resolved experimentally.
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures
♻ ☆ First-order Optimization Methods with Generalized Smoothness for Low-rank Matrix Factorization
A. V. Bidanets, F. S. Stonyakin
This paper studies several first-order methods for low-rank matrix minimization in the Burer--Monteiro form, where the target matrix is represented as the product of a nonnegative factor matrix and its transpose. Such a factorization destroys convexity of the objective function and global Lipschitz continuity of the gradient. We prove that for a quadratic objective function that is strongly convex only on the subspace of symmetric matrices, the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective possesses generalized smoothness with a fractional exponent 2/3. For a quadratic objective, the generalized smoothness property requires positive definiteness of the operator A only on the subspace of symmetric matrices, which relaxes the assumptions of Dragomir et al. On this basis, three methods are proposed: an adaptive gradient descent method with Armijo backtracking; an unconstrained SafeAdam method combining the Adam direction with a descent-angle certificate and a fallback to the normalized gradient; and a certified projected version for the nonnegativity constraint. Global convergence and explicit convergence rates for the proposed methods have been proved. The obtained convergence rate is better than the convergence rate of ordinary unaccelerated gradient descent in the case of a sufficiently large gradient. In the small-gradient regime, the convergence guarantee is of square-root type, and the corresponding complexity scales as the inverse square of the desired accuracy. In the large-gradient regime, the convergence guarantee is of three-quarters type, and the corresponding complexity is proportional to the inverse of the accuracy raised to the power of 4/3. Experiments on SymNMF using the TDT2, Reuters and CBCL datasets, which are standard benchmarks for document and image clustering, show that the methods match or outperform Dyn-NoLips without tuning the relative-smoothness kernel parameters.
♻ ☆ Two Answers on Heavy-Ball Dynamics
Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky, Martin Takáč
We determine the worst-case behavior of the heavy-ball method on smooth strongly convex functions, first for Polyak's quadratic-optimal parameters and then for arbitrary constant parameters. For Polyak's tuning, the exact dimension-uniform exponential rate is the largest growth factor of an interpolable mixture of rotating geometric sequences. Four algebraic families determine this rate at every condition number. Two frequencies suffice, and one function in dimension five attains the rate at every horizon up to constant factors. We recover the sharp convergence threshold $9+4\sqrt5$ of Badithela and Seiler. For general tunings, an exact linear feasibility criterion characterizes dimension-uniform linear convergence through the angle between the characteristic polynomials of the two extreme quadratics. This gives a continuous condition-number threshold and resolves the second heavy-ball riddle of Goujaud, Taylor and Dieuleveut. The regions between consecutive cycle tongues are Farey gaps, each containing convergent and divergent tunings. Regular portions of the threshold surface are analytic plateaus with fixed periodic frequency support. Every rational rotation number in a gap anchors a single-harmonic plateau; mixed-harmonic plateaus and an exact two-lag threshold point also occur. Along tongue edges, explicit multiplier inequalities and second-order expansions of competing Farey fans bound the transition from single-harmonic to mixed-harmonic extremals. The rate bounds and the extremal constructions follow from a common interpolation and separation argument that preserves initialization with zero momentum.

♻ ☆ Multi-cut stochastic approximation methods for solving stochastic convex composite optimization
Jiaming Liang, Renato D. C. Monteiro, Honghao Zhang
This paper considers the stochastic convex composite optimization problem and presents multi-cut stochastic approximation (SA) methods for solving it, whose models in expectation overestimate its objective function. The multi-cut model obtained by taking the maximum of a finite number of linearizations of the stochastic objective function provides a biased estimate of the objective function, with the error being uncontrollable. Instead, our proposed SA method uses models obtained by taking the maximum of a finite number of one-cut models, i.e., suitable convex combinations of linearizations of the stochastic objective function. It is shown that the proposed methods achieve nearly optimal convergence rate and have computational performance comparable, and sometimes superior, to other SA-type methods.
♻ ☆ Emission-aware operation of residential PV-battery systems: the role of information structure
Anna Sacilotto, Ambrogio Maria Bernardelli, Stefano Gualandi
Residential batteries can reduce the carbon emissions of households with photovoltaic (PV) generation, but how much depends on how they are operated under uncertain load, PV generation, and grid carbon intensity. We cast the operation of a residential PV-battery system as a sequential decision problem and compare, under a common and explicit evaluation protocol, a family of linear policies that differ in the information available at decision time, in how they anticipate the future, and in their adaptivity: a rule-based self-consumption policy, an open-loop stochastic schedule, affine feedback policies, receding-horizon policies with deterministic, scenario-based and two-stage lookahead models, and perfect-information benchmarks. Scenarios are generated by a joint principal component model of the three uncertain quantities, which supports conditional sampling during the day. Experiments on Italian data at 15-minute resolution comprise single-day evaluations on 10000 test scenarios in three seasons and a closed-loop simulation over more than eight months of real data. When the state of charge is treated consistently across policies, the self-consumption rule is within 3.2% of the perfect-foresight emissions in closed loop, whereas open-loop schedules and receding-horizon policies that decide before measuring the current period are about 20--35% above it. With real-time measurements, scenario-based receding-horizon control consistently outperforms its deterministic counterpart and, for households that rely more on the grid, reduces emissions by about 5% with respect to the rule. The benefit of emission-aware optimization is therefore determined mainly by the information structure of the controller and by the size of the system relative to the demand.
